blocks.text: Definition
Binary search is a searching algorithm that finds the position of a target value within a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search interval.
A condition that holds true before and after every iteration of the loop.
How it works
Find the middle element of the current interval.
Compare it with the target value.
If the target is smaller, search the left half; otherwise search the right half.
Repeat until the interval is empty or the target is found.
Preconditions
The array must be sorted.
Random access to elements must be possible.
Works on arrays and lists, not on linked lists.
Binary search on an unsorted array silently returns wrong answers rather than failing.
Complexity
O(log n)
Each comparison eliminates half of the remaining elements, so the number of steps grows logarithmically with the size of the input.
Searching a sorted array of 1,000,000 elements takes at most 20 comparisons.
Common mistake
Computing the midpoint as (low + high) / 2 can overflow for large indices. Use low + (high - low) / 2 instead.
The midpoint overflow bug existed in the Java standard library for nine years.
Although the basic idea is simple, the details can be surprisingly tricky.
